latin.2553: CXVI. Sed inter Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae multi sunt qui mediam quodammodo viam insistunt, inter sententiam Molinae, & inter sententiam Thomistarum recentiorum, quae videntur quasi in extremo positae. Quamvis enim quod ad rei summam cum Molina sentiant, in quibusdam tamen ab eo discedunt, & doctrinam ejus emollire conantur. Quo de numero sunt Bellarminus & Vasquez, ac praecipue Petrus a Sancto Joseph Fuliensis Monachus.
latin.2554: CXVII. Primo enim cum Molina existimant dari quandam gratiam sufficientem, ad hominis salutem & conversionem, per quam, licet homo actu non convertatur, potest tamen, si voluerit illa uti, actu converti, sine ullo alio praevio Dei auxilio. Nec putant eam gratiam sufficientem recte dici, praeter quam aliud Dei auxilium ad bonam actionem praecedaneum requiritur, ut actio reapse sequatur.
latin.2555: CXVIII. Id docet Petrus ille a Sancto Joseph in tractatu Theologico de gratia Divina Disputatione 6. Sectione 6. Ubi haec est ejus prima assertio. Certum est ex fide dari gratiam aliquam sufficientem ad salutem, qua scilicet homo converti possit, licet actu non convertatur. Secunda vero sic se habet. Ea gratia dicitur sufficiens, quae sufficit non tantum ut homo operari possit, sed etiam ut actu operetur si velit.
latin.2556: CXIX. Quam Doctrinam repetit & confirmat in Idea Theologiae speculativae libro quarto cap. 7. Ubi haec est ejus Resolutio 2. Ea tantum gratia dicitur absolute, & vere sufficiens ad aliquam operationem, quae sufficit non tantum ut homo dicatur utcunque posse operari, sed etiam ut actu operetur, si velit. Quod dicit se statuere contra authores Physicae praedeterminationis, qui volunt auxilium illud esse vere sufficiens ad operationem, quod tribuit posse operari, etsi necessario requiratur aliud auxilium realiter a sufficienti distinctum, ut quis actu operetur. Nec enim, exempli causa, hominem aliter dici habere sufficientem & proximam potestatem ad videndum, nisi quia habet quicquid requiritur ut actu videat, si videre velit.
latin.2557: CXX. Secundo pertendunt, cum eodem Molina, nullam Dei gratiam sic efficacem esse, ut voluntatem ad bene agendum Physice praedeterminet, & sic ut aliquam imponat agendi necessitatem, quae sit ad bonam ipsam actionem antecedens. Nec enim censent ullam talem necessitatem cum arbitrii humani libertate consistere posse. Quanquam alioqui non negent gratiam Physice movere & inclinare voluntatem ad bonas operationes.
latin.2558: CXXI. Id videre est apud Petrum istum a Sancto Joseph tractatus jam citati disputatione septima, quam pene totam insumit in refutanda gratiae Physica praedeterminatione. Et in idea quoque Theologiae speculativae capite illo septimo libri quarti. Ubi haec ejus est sexta Resolutio. Etsi juxta probabilem sententiam, gratia efficax realiter, & Physice voluntatem moveat & inclinet ad opus bonum, non tamen ad illud eam Physice praedeterminat. Cujus Resolutionis primam partem inde probat quod gratia efficax est motio quaedam realis in anima existens, eamque, veluti per modum cujusdam impetus impressi, ad opus bonum inclinans: quare sicut in rebus corporeis, impetus effective & realiter ad motum localem concurrit; ita proportione servata, impetus voluntati impressus ad motus spirituales, & supernaturales animae realiter cooperari debet.
latin.2559: CXXII. Praeterea quum explicant quid sit gratia efficax, per quam homines actu convertuntur, illam constituunt in eadem mentis illuminatione, iisdemque voluntatis motibus atque affectibus, in quibus juxta Molinam posita est. Nam gratiam efficacem nolunt esse quid realiter distinctum a gratia excitante, sive praeveniente, quae secundum illos consistit tum in variis inspirationibus & illuminationibus intellectus, quibus mens incipit cogitare de praemio vitae aeternae, poenis inferni, pulchritudine virtutis, &c. tum in variis affectibus voluntati divinitus immissis, quibus incipit amare bona coelestia, poenas tartareas timere, affici erga virtutem, &c. ut apud Petrum a Sancto Joseph legere est tractatu de gratia divina disp. 7. sect. 1. Hi enim motus, inquit, alliciunt voluntatem, eique vires tribuunt ad consentiendum, & consentientem juvant ad consensum, cum illa effective concurrendo.
latin.2560: CXXIII. Caeterum quanquam in rebus iisdem cum Molina ponant gratiam efficacem, eodem modo tamen non explicant in quo consistat ejus efficacia. Nam ut supra fuit fuse expositum, Molina vult gratiam efficacem dici ab eventu, quia voluntas humana ei cooperatur; adeoque secundum illius hypotheses, efficacia gratiae simpliciter pendet a libero hominis arbitrio, in cujus potestate est gratiam quae ex se sufficiens tantum est, vel efficacem, vel inefficacem reddere. Et sic consequenter viri istius principiis dicendum est gratiae efficaciam consistere in assensu & cooperatione voluntatis humanae. Hoc autem diserte negant Doctores illi quorum sententiam exponimus. Ac pertendunt gratiam quae efficax dicitur, ex se ante consensum voluntatis esse efficacem: nec si proprie loquendum sit, gratiam efficacem esse, quia voluntas consentit; sed potius ideo voluntatem consentire quia gratia efficax est.
latin.2561: CXXIV. Haec est expressa Bellarmini Doctrina libro primo de Gratia & Libero Arbitrio cap. 12. ubi postquam retulit opinionem eorum, qui gratiam efficacem constituunt in assensu & cooperatione humana, ita ut ab eventu dicatur gratia efficax, quia voluntas humana cooperatur; quique existimant in potestate hominis esse, ut gratiam faciat esse efficacem, quae alioquin ex se non esset nisi sufficiens: subjungit, Haec opinio aliena est omnino a sententia Beati Augustini, & quantum ego existimo a sententiis etiam scripturarum divinarum. Et similiter Petrus a Sancto Joseph hanc ponit assertionem, Efficacia gratiae non consistit in cooperatione voluntatis. De gratia Divina disputat. 7. Sectione 9. num. 61. Efficaciam autem gratiae non consistere in illa voluntatis cooperatione probat, quia non ideo gratia est efficax, quia voluntas operatur; quin potius ideo voluntas operatur, quia gratia est efficax. Ac proinde efficacia gratiae non potest formaliter sumi a cooperatione voluntatis, cum sit causa illius, eamque praecedat. In Idea Theol. specul. l. 4. cap. 7. ad 7. Resolutionem.

sections.title: A middle way between Molina and the recent Thomists
sections.pass_a: CXVI. But among the Doctors of the Roman Church there are many who keep a middle way as it were, between the opinion of Molina, & the opinion of the recent Thomists, which seem placed as it were at the extremes. For although as to the sum of the matter they agree with Molina, yet in some things they depart from him, & try to soften his doctrine. Of which number are Bellarmine & Vasquez, and especially Peter of Saint Joseph, a Feuillant Monk.
pass_b: Thesis CXVI. Among the doctors of the Roman Church, however, many take what is in a sense a middle way between Molina's view and that of the recent Thomists, which seem to stand, as it were, at the extremes. For although on the substance of the question they agree with Molina, they depart from him on some points and try to soften his doctrine. Among them are Bellarmine and Vasquez, and above all Peter of Saint Joseph, a Feuillant monk.

sections.title: First: sufficient grace suffices for actual conversion
sections.pass_a: CXVII. For first with Molina they think that there is given a certain sufficient grace, for man's salvation & conversion, by which, although man is not actually converted, he can yet, if he will use it, be actually converted, without any other prior aid of God. Nor do they think that grace rightly called sufficient, beyond which another aid of God going before the good action is required, that the action may really follow.
pass_b: Thesis CXVII. First, they hold with Molina that a sufficient grace is given for a person's salvation and conversion. Even if he is not actually converted, he can still be actually converted through it, if he chooses to use it, without any further prior aid from God. A grace that needs some other preceding aid of God before the good action really follows is not, in their view, properly called sufficient.

sections.title: Peter of Saint Joseph on sufficient grace
sections.pass_a: CXVIII. This Peter of Saint Joseph teaches in the Theological treatise on divine grace Disputation 6. Section 6. Where this is his first assertion. It is certain from faith that there is given some sufficient grace to salvation, by which namely a man can be converted, although he be not actually converted. But the second runs thus. That grace is called sufficient, which suffices not only that a man can work, but also that he actually work if he will.
pass_b: Thesis CXVIII. Peter of Saint Joseph teaches this in his theological treatise on divine grace, disputation 6, section 6, where his first assertion reads: 'It is certain from faith that some grace sufficient for salvation is given, a grace by which a person can be converted even though he is not actually converted.' His second is this: 'That grace is called sufficient which is enough not only for a person to be able to act, but also for him actually to act if he chooses.'

sections.title: Sufficient means enough to act, if one wills
sections.pass_a: CXIX. Which Doctrine he repeats & confirms in the Idea of speculative Theology book four chap. 7. Where this is his Resolution 2. That grace alone is called absolutely, & truly sufficient for some operation, which suffices not only that a man be said in some way to be able to work, but also that he actually work, if he will. Which he says he establishes against the authors of Physical predetermination, who will have that aid to be truly sufficient for operation, which gives the power to work, although there be necessarily required another aid really distinct from the sufficient, that one may actually work. For neither, for example, is a man otherwise said to have sufficient & proximate power for seeing, except because he has whatever is required that he actually see, if he will to see.
pass_b: Thesis CXIX. He repeats and confirms this doctrine in his Idea of speculative theology, book 4, chapter 7, where his second resolution reads: 'Only that grace is called absolutely and truly sufficient for some operation which is enough not merely for a person to be said to be able to act in some fashion, but also for him actually to act, if he chooses.'

He says he lays this down against the authors of physical predetermination. They hold that an aid is truly sufficient for operation if it gives the ability to act, even though another aid, really distinct from the sufficient one, is necessarily required for anyone actually to act. For, to take an example, a person is said to have sufficient and proximate power to see only because he has everything needed to see in fact, if he wants to see.

sections.title: Second: no grace physically predetermines the will
sections.pass_a: CXX. Secondly they contend, with the same Molina, that no grace of God is so efficacious, as to predetermine the will Physically to acting well, & so as to impose some necessity of acting, which is antecedent to the good action itself. For they do not think that any such necessity can consist with the liberty of human choice. Although otherwise they do not deny that grace Physically moves & inclines the will to good operations.
pass_b: Thesis CXX. Second, they maintain with Molina that no grace of God is efficacious in the sense of physically predetermining the will to act well and so imposing a necessity of acting that comes before the good action itself. In their view no such necessity can coexist with the freedom of human choice. They do not deny, on the other hand, that grace moves and inclines the will physically toward good operations.

sections.title: Peter of Saint Joseph against physical predetermination
sections.pass_a: CXXI. This is to be seen in this Peter of Saint Joseph in the seventh disputation of the treatise already cited, which he spends almost wholly in refuting the Physical predetermination of grace. And also in the idea of speculative Theology in that seventh chapter of the fourth book. Where this is his sixth Resolution. Although according to the probable opinion, efficacious grace really, & Physically moves & inclines the will to the good work, yet it does not Physically predetermine it to it. The first part of which Resolution he proves from this, that efficacious grace is a certain real motion existing in the soul, and inclining it, as by the manner of a certain impressed impetus, to the good work: wherefore as in bodily things, impetus concurs effectively & really to local motion; so, proportion being kept, the impetus impressed on the will ought really to cooperate in the spiritual, & supernatural motions of the soul.
pass_b: Thesis CXXI. This can be seen in Peter of Saint Joseph, in the seventh disputation of the treatise already cited, which he devotes almost entirely to refuting the physical predetermination of grace, and also in the same seventh chapter of book 4 of the Idea of speculative theology. His sixth resolution there reads: 'Although, on the probable view, efficacious grace really and physically moves and inclines the will to the good work, it does not physically predetermine it to that work.'

He proves the first part of this resolution from the claim that efficacious grace is a real motion existing in the soul, inclining it to the good work after the manner of an impressed impetus. In bodies an impetus concurs effectively and really in local motion; so, by proportion, the impetus impressed on the will must really cooperate in the soul's spiritual and supernatural motions.

sections.title: Third: efficacious grace placed in the same things as Molina's
sections.pass_a: CXXII. Moreover when they explain what efficacious grace is, by which men are actually converted, they place it in the same illumination of the mind, and the same motions & affections of the will, in which according to Molina it is placed. For they will not have efficacious grace to be something really distinct from exciting grace, or prevenient, which according to them consists both in various inspirations & illuminations of the intellect, by which the mind begins to think of the reward of eternal life, the punishments of hell, the beauty of virtue, &c. and in various affections sent into the will by God, by which it begins to love heavenly goods, to fear the punishments of hell, to be affected toward virtue, &c. as may be read in Peter of Saint Joseph in the treatise on divine grace disp. 7. sect. 1. For these motions, he says, allure the will, and give it strength for consenting, & help it when consenting to consent, concurring with it effectively.
pass_b: Thesis CXXII. Further, when they explain what efficacious grace is, the grace by which people are actually converted, they place it in the same illumination of the mind and the same motions and affections of the will in which Molina places it. They will not have efficacious grace be anything really distinct from exciting or prevenient grace.

On their account that grace consists, on the one hand, in various inspirations and illuminations of the intellect, by which the mind begins to think about the reward of eternal life, the pains of hell, the beauty of virtue and so on; and, on the other, in various affections sent by God into the will, by which it begins to love heavenly goods, to fear the pains of hell, to be drawn toward virtue and so on. So one reads in Peter of Saint Joseph, treatise on divine grace, disputation 7, section 1: 'These motions,' he says, 'entice the will, give it the strength to consent, and help it, once it consents, to give its consent, by concurring with it effectively.'

sections.title: But efficacy does not consist in consent
sections.pass_a: CXXIII. However although they place efficacious grace in the same things with Molina, yet they do not explain in the same way in what its efficacy consists. For as was set out at length above, Molina will have grace called efficacious from the outcome, because the human will cooperates with it; and so according to his hypotheses, the efficacy of grace depends simply on man's free choice, in whose power it is to render grace which of itself is only sufficient, either efficacious, or inefficacious. And so consequently on that man's principles it must be said that the efficacy of grace consists in the assent & cooperation of the human will. But this the Doctors whose opinion we are setting out expressly deny. And they contend that the grace which is called efficacious, is efficacious of itself before the consent of the will: nor, if one is to speak properly, is grace efficacious, because the will consents; but rather the will consents for this reason because grace is efficacious.
pass_b: Thesis CXXIII. These writers locate efficacious grace in the very things Molina names, but they give a different account of where its efficacy lies. Molina, as shown at length earlier, has grace called efficacious on account of its result, namely that the human will works along with it. His assumptions therefore make the efficacy of grace hang simply on man's free choice, which can turn a grace that is in itself merely sufficient into an efficacious or an inefficacious one; and it follows from his principles that efficacy consists in the human will's assent and cooperation.

That conclusion is flatly rejected by the doctors whose position is being described here. They insist that the grace called efficacious is efficacious of itself, before the will consents. Properly speaking, grace is not efficacious because the will gives its consent; the will gives its consent because grace is efficacious.

sections.title: Bellarmine and Peter of Saint Joseph against efficacy from cooperation
sections.pass_a: CXXIV. This is the express Doctrine of Bellarmine in the first book on Grace & Free Choice chap. 12. where after he has reported the opinion of those, who place efficacious grace in human assent & cooperation, so that grace is called efficacious from the outcome, because the human will cooperates; and who think it is in man's power, to make grace be efficacious, which otherwise of itself would be only sufficient: he adds, This opinion is altogether foreign to the opinion of Blessed Augustine, & as far as I judge to the opinions also of the divine scriptures. And likewise Peter of Saint Joseph lays down this assertion, The efficacy of grace does not consist in the cooperation of the will. On divine Grace disputat. 7. Section 9. num. 61. And he proves that the efficacy of grace does not consist in that cooperation of the will, because grace is not efficacious for this reason, because the will works; but rather the will works for this reason, because grace is efficacious. And therefore the efficacy of grace cannot formally be taken from the cooperation of the will, since it is the cause of it, and precedes it. In the Idea of spec. Theol. b. 4. chap. 7. on the 7. Resolution.
pass_b: Thesis CXXIV. This is Bellarmine's express doctrine in book 1 of On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 12. He first reports the view of those who place efficacious grace in human assent and cooperation, so that grace is called efficacious from its outcome because the human will cooperates, and who think it lies in a person's power to make grace efficacious when of itself it would be only sufficient. Then he adds: 'This opinion is wholly foreign to the teaching of blessed Augustine and, as I judge, to the teaching of the divine Scriptures as well.'

Peter of Saint Joseph likewise lays down this assertion: 'The efficacy of grace does not consist in the cooperation of the will' (On divine grace, disputation 7, section 9, number 61). He proves it on the ground that grace is not efficacious because the will acts; on the contrary, the will acts because grace is efficacious. The efficacy of grace therefore cannot formally be taken from the will's cooperation, since that efficacy is the cause of the cooperation and comes before it (Idea of speculative theology, book 4, chapter 7, on the seventh resolution).
